name: Occipital pole
summary: The occipital pole is the posterior tip of the hemisphere where the calcarine sulcus reaches the surface and the primary visual cortex spreads onto the lateral convexity, representing the central visual field (the macula) with a huge cortical magnification. It receives a dual blood supply from the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery and from the terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery, which is why the macula is spared in many PCA infarcts and why the pole is selectively damaged in watershed injury and in hypotension. Bilateral polar lesions cause central scotomas and loss of reading, and the pole is the site of the visual auras of occipital epilepsy and of the release hallucinations of visual loss.

anatomy.location: Posterior extremity of the hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and the preoccipital notch, where the medial, lateral and inferior surfaces of the occipital lobe converge; the calcarine sulcus ends here and the macular representation extends onto the lateral surface.

function: The posterior calcarine cortex at the pole receives the foveal projection, with the central few degrees occupying as much cortex as the whole peripheral field, and analyzes the fine detail, color and stereopsis needed for reading, face recognition and skilled hand work; it feeds the fusiform and lateral occipital areas that identify letters and objects. The vertical meridian is represented at the border with the opposite hemisphere through the splenium, and the pole contributes to the maintenance of fixation and to the smallest voluntary saccades. Its loss on one side produces a congruous contralateral paracentral scotoma or a hemianopia without macular sparing.

bestView.label: occipital pole with the macular representation
posterior tip of the hemisphere at the end of the calcarine sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: Rounded posterior tip of the hemisphere on axial and sagittal images, where the calcarine sulcus reaches the surface; the poles are often asymmetric with one petalia projecting further back, a normal variant.

pathology.finding: Bilateral restricted diffusion of the occipital tips after hypotension or cardiac arrest with central scotomas and impaired reading despite preserved peripheral fields.
Calcarine infarct extending to the pole when the MCA collateral is poor, producing a complete hemianopia without macular sparing.
Central colored or flashing auras, ictal blindness or amaurosis, occipital spikes increased by eye closure.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral paracentral scotoma or hemianopia without macular sparing
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the foveal representation at the occipital pole

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral central scotomas and impaired reading
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral polar damage in border-zone injury
Ictal activation of the macular cortex

examination: Central fields with a red target and the Amsler grid
Reading acuity in addition to distance acuity
Perimetry for paracentral and macular defects
pearls: The macula has two arteries; the occipital pole is spared by a PCA stroke and hit by a hypotensive one
Bilateral occipital pole infarcts give a patient who walks confidently but cannot read
Occipital petalia (one pole projecting further back) is a normal asymmetry seen on every MRI

pitfalls: Macular sparing is not a sign of a benign lesion; it only reflects the dual blood supply of the pole
